own_scenes.desc: Los rumores de la muerte del metal eran exagerados: fuera del mercado estadounidense y en el underground está más vivo que nunca. El capitalismo global crea clases obreras industriales cuyos jóvenes buscan identidad en la cultura popular, y el metal llega a todos los países industriales: Tang Dynasty en la MTV asiática, Modar en Malasia (donde el gobierno prohíbe el metal en 1993 por presión islamista), Indonesia y Singapur, Brasil, Chile, Argentina y México, e incluso Malta, Israel, Islandia y Egipto. Ese público mundial preservó el metal para Estados Unidos como los monasterios la sabiduría antigua. El underground, como el Purgatorio o el Infierno de Dante, nace con MTV como su gemelo malvado: sin baladas ni poses, con estructuras complejas, el bien y el mal y voces gruñidas. Lo sostienen sellos de origen europeo (Century Media, Earache, Nuclear Blast, Roadrunner, Relapse), cientos de programas de radio universitaria, revistas de todo el mundo (Terrorizer, Rock Hard, Metal Maniacs, Burrn!, Rock Brigade…), festivales (Metalfest de Milwaukee, Dynamo en Holanda, Monsters of Rock en América Latina) e internet: webs, e-zines, grupos de noticias y radios en línea. Es mayor en Europa, donde hay subsidios juveniles, locales de ensayo públicos y una identidad obrera más fuerte, y en Estados Unidos lo frenan las leyes sobre el alcohol y las grandes cadenas que no venden discos «insanos».

refs.q: It turned out that the rumors of metal’s death were greatly exaggerated
refs.para: There was no agreement about the cause of metal’s death and no one ever did find the body; its existence was inferred from the absence of metal on the U.S. Billboard charts (see Appendix C). It turned out that the rumors of metal’s death were greatly exaggerated; metal is alive and well, thriving as a creative art form with an enthusiastic fan base outside the U.S. mainstream market. Metal flourishes throughout the rest of the world and in the aptly named underground.
refs.chapter: Cap. 8: El metal en los noventa

refs.q: In the mid-’90s Asian MTV gave heavy airplay to Tang Dynasty, a mainland Chinese heavy-metal band.
refs.para: Beyond Japan, hotbeds of metal fans arose in some of the newly industrialized Pacific Rim countries. In the mid-’90s Asian MTV gave heavy airplay to Tang Dynasty, a mainland Chinese heavy-metal band.¹⁷ Young men in Malaysia, Indonesia, and Singapore started their own musical careers. Modar, a death-metal band, comes from one of Malaysia’s most conservative areas. In 1993, the Malaysian government banned live performances and airplay of heavy metal. refs.q: Underground metal began when MTV did, as its evil twin, embodying everything MTV metal was not.
refs.para: Underground metal began when MTV did, as its evil twin, embodying everything MTV metal was not. It is devoid of pop tropes like ballads and star posturing. Its lyrics lack romantic fluff, hippie hopefulness, or Gen-X self-pity. The music is anything but simplistic, with complex time changes and chord progressions. The underground continues metal’s original obsession with good and evil, verbally depicted in ways that would defrost Walt Disney’s cryogenic tomb. Not that the words can be easily understood; in some styles, singing is best described as growling or screeching.
refs.chapter: Cap. 8: El metal en los noventa

refs.q: The metal underground has been flourishing since the mid–1990s in large measure through the internet.
refs.para: The metal underground has been flourishing since the mid–1990s in large measure through the internet. Whether the sites are made by fans, band members, or indie labels, they provide a wealth of information, including band histories, reviews and interviews, lyrics, pictures, sound clips, and links to related sites. The internet also allows indie labels to promote their new releases at little cost. With worldwide distribution and no printing or mailing expenses, magazines on the net (e-’zines) abound. Opinions on underground metal are also found on dozens of news groups (like alt.rock-n-roll.metal.heavy or alt.rock-n-roll.metal.black) where a wide variety of issues are discussed, albums and bootlegs are traded, and information on new releases, tour dates, set lists, and new web sites are posted. In some sense, the internet helps to form a virtual community of fans.
